source.text: לַמְנַצֵּ֥חַ בִּנְגִינֹ֗ת מַשְׂכִּ֥יל לְדָוִֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: For the director, with stringed instruments, a maskil of David.

en.L: For the director: with stringed instruments. A maskil of David.
en.B: For the music director. With stringed instruments. A maskil of David.
en.R: For the leader of the music. To be played on stringed instruments. A song by David to teach and give insight.

decisions.reason: The title is part of the Hebrew text and is counted as verse 1, so the verse numbers here are one higher than in Bibles that print the title without a number.

decisions.choice: the director: the one who leads the music
decisions.reason: As in 4:1, probably the leader of the temple music.

decisions.choice: stringed instruments: to be accompanied on strings
decisions.reason: As in 4:1, the word (neginot) is used for music played on strings; it tells how the psalm was to be performed.

decisions.choice: maskil: probably a skillful or instructive song
decisions.reason: As in 32:1, the word (maskil) comes from a verb meaning to be wise or to give insight. Its exact sense as a kind of song is no longer known.

decisions.choice: a song to teach and give insight
decisions.reason: Readable gives the likely sense of the term, as in 42:1.

source.text: הַאֲזִ֣ינָה אֱ֭לֹהִים תְּפִלָּתִ֑י וְאַל־תִּ֝תְעַלַּ֗ם מִתְּחִנָּתִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Give ear, God, [to] my prayer, and do not hide yourself from my plea for favor.

en.L: Give ear, God, to my prayer, and do not hide {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}} from my plea for favor.
en.B: God, listen to my prayer; do not close {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes to my plea.
en.R: God, listen to my prayer. Please do not turn away when I beg {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} for help.

decisions.choice: hide yourself: look the other way
decisions.reason: The verb is used of ignoring someone in need, as in Isaiah 58:7: to see and choose not to help.

decisions.choice: plea for favor: a plea for grace
decisions.reason: The word (techinnah) is a plea for favor one has no claim to, from the verb "be gracious".

decisions.choice: do not close your eyes (B); do not turn away (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m1).

source.text: הַקְשִׁ֣יבָה לִּ֣י וַעֲנֵ֑נִי אָרִ֖יד בְּשִׂיחִ֣י וְאָהִֽימָה׃

records.literal_gloss: Pay attention to me and answer me; I wander in my complaint and I moan,

en.L: Pay attention to me and answer me; I wander restless in my complaint, and I moan,
en.B: Listen to me and answer me. My worries leave me no rest, and I groan aloud,
en.R: Please pay attention and answer me. My troubles give me no rest. I am upset and groaning.

decisions.reason: The verb (rud) means to roam about; here it is the restlessness of a troubled mind.
The word (siach) is anxious thought and the words that pour it out (64:2; 142:3).
Verse 4 says why he groans, so this verse ends with a comma at Literal and Balanced.

decisions.choice: My worries leave me no rest (B); My troubles give me no rest (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense (m1, m2).

source.text: מִקּ֤וֹל אוֹיֵ֗ב מִפְּנֵ֣י עָקַ֣ת רָשָׁ֑ע כִּי־יָמִ֥יטוּ עָלַ֥י אָ֝֗וֶן וּבְאַ֥ף יִשְׂטְמֽוּנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: because of [the] voice of [the] enemy, because of [the] pressure of [the] wicked; for they drop on me trouble, and in anger they bear a grudge against me.

en.L: because of the voice of the enemy, because of the pressure of the wicked; for they let trouble fall on me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me.
en.B: at the shouting of the enemy and the crushing weight of the wicked; for they bring trouble crashing down on me, and in their anger they nurse a grudge against me.
en.R: This is because my enemy shouts at me and wicked people press hard on me. They pile trouble on me. They are angry and hate me.

decisions.reason: The word ('aqah) is found only here; from a root meaning to press, it is the weight the wicked put on him.

decisions.choice: drop trouble on me: bring harm down on me
decisions.reason: The verb (mot) means to make something topple; they let trouble ('awen) fall on him like stones from a wall. The word 'awen can also mean wrongdoing, so they may be loading false charges on him.
The verb (satam) is used of Esau's grudge against Jacob (Genesis 27:41).
Readable starts a new sentence and links it to verse 3.

source.text: לִ֭בִּי יָחִ֣יל בְּקִרְבִּ֑י וְאֵימ֥וֹת מָ֝֗וֶת נָפְל֥וּ עָלָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: My heart writhes within me, and terrors of death have fallen on me.

en.L: My heart writhes within me, and terrors of death have fallen on me.
en.B: My heart twists in pain inside me; the dread of death has come down on me.
en.R: My heart is pounding with fear. I am terrified that I am going to die.

decisions.reason: The verb (chil) is used of a woman in labor (48:7): pain that grips the whole body.

decisions.choice: terrors of death: the fear of dying
decisions.reason: The threats of verse 4 make death feel near.

decisions.choice: I am terrified that I am going to die
alternatives: terrors of death have fallen on me
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means (m2).

source.text: יִרְאָ֣ה וָ֭רַעַד יָ֣בֹא בִ֑י וַ֝תְּכַסֵּ֗נִי פַּלָּצֽוּת׃

records.literal_gloss: Fear and trembling come on me, and horror has covered me.

en.L: Fear and trembling come on me, and horror has covered me.
en.B: Fear and trembling take hold of me; I am wrapped in horror.
en.R: I am afraid, and I cannot stop shaking. Terror has taken over my whole body.

decisions.reason: The word (pallatsut) is a shuddering of fear (Job 21:6; Isaiah 21:4).
Horror covers him like a garment or like water over the head.

source.text: וָאֹמַ֗ר מִֽי־יִתֶּן־לִּ֣י אֵ֭בֶר כַּיּוֹנָ֗ה אָע֥וּפָה וְאֶשְׁכֹּֽנָה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I said, Who will give to me a wing like the dove! I would fly away and settle down.

en.L: And I said, "Who will give me wings like the dove! I would fly away and settle down.
en.B: I said, "If only I had a dove's wings! I would fly off and settle somewhere far away.
en.R: I said, "I wish I had a dove's wings. Then I could fly far off and find a place to rest.

decisions.reason: As in 14:7, "Who will give ...?" expresses a wish.

decisions.choice: the dove: a bird that flies far and hides
decisions.reason: Doves fly fast and nest in the clefts of high rocks (Jeremiah 48:28), out of reach. Compare 11:1, "Flee like a bird to your mountain".

decisions.choice: I said: the speech runs to verse 9
decisions.reason: What he said runs through verse 9, so the quotation closes there.

decisions.choice: settle down: find a home, be at rest
decisions.reason: The verb (shakan) means to settle and live in a place.

source.text: הִ֭נֵּה אַרְחִ֣יק נְדֹ֑ד אָלִ֖ין בַּמִּדְבָּ֣ר סֶֽלָה׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, I would go far away fleeing; I would lodge in the wilderness. Selah.

en.L: Look, I would go far away in flight; I would lodge in the wilderness. Selah
en.B: See, I would run far off and spend my nights in the wilderness. Selah
en.R: I would run far away and stay out in the wilderness. Selah

decisions.reason: The dry, thinly settled land east and south of Jerusalem, where David once hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14). It stands for a place far from people.
The verb (lin) is to stay overnight, as a traveler does.

decisions.choice: Selah: a word whose meaning is no longer known
alternatives: lift up (the voice or the music)
decisions.reason: Selah stands at the end of a line 71 times in the Psalms and 3 times in Habakkuk 3. It is probably a direction for singing or music, perhaps a pause or an interlude; the ancient Greek translation renders it with a word meaning "interlude". It is not part of what is said, and here it marks a break after the line.
Its meaning is unknown (see the meaning decision on Selah), so every level keeps the word rather than guess, and keeps it apart from the sentence.

source.text: אָחִ֣ישָׁה מִפְלָ֣ט לִ֑י מֵר֖וּחַ סֹעָ֣ה מִסָּֽעַר׃

records.literal_gloss: I would hurry [to] a place of escape for me from [the] rushing wind, from [the] storm.

en.L: I would hurry to my place of escape, from the rushing wind, from the storm."
en.B: I would hurry to a refuge of my own, away from the raging wind and the storm."
en.R: I would rush to a safe place, away from the wild wind and the storm."

decisions.choice: wind and storm: the trouble from which he longs to escape
decisions.reason: The storm is the turmoil caused by his enemies (83:16; Isaiah 25:4).

decisions.choice: a place of escape: a refuge
decisions.reason: The word (miflat) is a place where one is safe (18:3).

source.text: בַּלַּ֣ע אֲ֭דֹנָי פַּלַּ֣ג לְשׁוֹנָ֑ם כִּֽי־רָאִ֨יתִי חָמָ֖ס וְרִ֣יב בָּעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: Swallow, Lord, divide their tongue, for I have seen violence and strife in the city.

en.L: Swallow [them] up, my Lord, divide their tongue, for I have seen violence and strife in the city.
en.B: Lord, bring them to nothing and split their speech, because I have seen violence and quarreling all through the city.
en.R: Lord, destroy their plans. Confuse their words so they cannot agree. I see people hurting each other and fighting everywhere in the city.

decisions.reason: The verb (bala') means to swallow up and so to destroy; with plans it means to confound them (Isaiah 19:3).

decisions.choice: divide their tongue: as at Babel
decisions.reason: At Babel God confused the builders' language so that they could not work together (Genesis 11:7-9); the verb "divide" (palag) is the root of the name Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided (Genesis 10:25).
The city is not named. The walls, the square and the house of God (verses 11-15) suggest Jerusalem.
In address, "Lord" carries the sense of "my Lord" ('Adonai); Literal keeps "my".

decisions.choice: destroy their plans; confuse their words so they cannot agree
decisions.reason: Readable explains the two pictures (m1, m2).

source.text: יוֹמָ֤ם וָלַ֗יְלָה יְסוֹבְבֻ֥הָ עַל־חוֹמֹתֶ֑יהָ וְאָ֖וֶן וְעָמָ֣ל בְּקִרְבָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: By day and night they go around it on its walls, and wickedness and trouble [are] in its midst.

en.L: Day and night they circle it upon its walls, and wickedness and trouble [are] in its midst.
en.B: Day and night violence and strife make their rounds on its walls, and evil and misery fill the city.
en.R: Day and night, violence and fighting walk along the city walls like guards. Evil and trouble are everywhere inside.

decisions.reason: "They" most naturally refers to violence and strife (verse 10), pictured as watchmen patrolling the walls. Instead of guards keeping the city safe, evil keeps watch over it.

decisions.choice: wickedness and trouble: evil and the misery it causes
decisions.reason: The same pair as in 10:7.

decisions.choice: violence and strife (B); violence and fighting (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name what "they" are (m1).
Readable says what the picture is (m1).

source.text: הַוּ֥וֹת בְּקִרְבָּ֑הּ וְֽלֹא־יָמִ֥ישׁ מֵ֝רְחֹבָ֗הּ תֹּ֣ךְ וּמִרְמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Destruction [is] in its midst, and does not depart from its square oppression and deceit.

en.L: Destruction [is] in its midst, and oppression and deceit do not depart from its square.
en.B: Ruin is at its center; cruelty and lies never leave its public square.
en.R: The city is full of things that ruin people. In the marketplace, people are always being cheated and treated cruelly.

decisions.choice: its square: the open place of trade and justice
decisions.reason: The square (rechov) was the open space inside the city gate where people traded, met and held courts (Nehemiah 8:1). Where justice should be done, oppression rules.
The word (tokh) goes with deceit also in 10:7.
As in 52:4 (hawwot).

source.text: כִּ֤י לֹֽא־אוֹיֵ֥ב יְחָֽרְפֵ֗נִי וְאֶ֫שָּׂ֥א לֹֽא־מְ֭שַׂנְאִי עָלַ֣י הִגְדִּ֑יל וְאֶסָּתֵ֥ר מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For not an enemy taunts me, and I could bear [it]; not one who hates me has magnified himself against me, and I could hide from him.

en.L: For [it is] not an enemy [who] taunts me, or I could bear [it]; [it is] not one who hates me [who] has made himself great against me, or I could hide from him.
en.B: The one who mocks me is not an enemy, or I could bear it; the one who lords it over me is not someone who hates me, or I could keep out of his way.
en.R: The person who insults me is not an enemy. If it were, I could stand it. It is not someone who hates me who acts so proud against me. If it were, I could hide from him.

decisions.choice: and I could bear it: what he could do if it were so
decisions.reason: The verbs in the unfinished form say what would be possible if the attacker were an open enemy.

decisions.choice: made himself great against me: treated me with contempt
decisions.reason: To make oneself great against someone is to rise up arrogantly against them (35:26).

decisions.choice: an enemy, one who hates me: the betrayer was a friend
decisions.reason: Verses 14-15 say who it really is.

source.text: וְאַתָּ֣ה אֱנ֣וֹשׁ כְּעֶרְכִּ֑י אַ֝לּוּפִ֗י וּמְיֻדָּֽעִי׃

records.literal_gloss: And you, a man according to my value, my close friend and my known one,

en.L: But you, a man according to my rank, my close friend and my intimate,
en.B: But it is you, a man of my own standing, my friend and my trusted companion,
en.R: But it is you, someone just like me, my close friend. We knew each other so well.

decisions.choice: according to my value: my equal
decisions.reason: The word ('erekh) is a valuation or rank (Leviticus 27:2). The friend was David's equal, not a servant.

decisions.choice: close friend, known one: a trusted intimate
decisions.reason: The first word ('alluf) is a close friend (Proverbs 16:28); the second (meyudda') is someone well known, a confidant (31:12).

decisions.choice: you: a friend who betrayed him
decisions.reason: The psalm does not name him. David's counselor Ahithophel, who joined Absalom's revolt, is one example of such a friend (2 Samuel 15:12, 31).
Verse 15 continues the description, so this verse ends with a comma at Literal and Balanced.

source.text: אֲשֶׁ֣ר יַ֭חְדָּו נַמְתִּ֣יק ס֑וֹד בְּבֵ֥ית אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים נְהַלֵּ֥ךְ בְּרָֽגֶשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: who together we made sweet counsel; in [the] house of God we walked in [the] throng.

en.L: with whom together we made counsel sweet; in the house of God we walked in the throng.
en.B: we used to share our hearts as friends, and we walked with the crowd at the house of God.
en.R: We used to talk together as close friends. We walked together with the crowds of worshipers at God's house.

decisions.reason: The word (sod) is the private talk of trusted friends (25:14).

decisions.choice: the throng: the crowds of worshipers
decisions.reason: The festival crowds going to God's house (42:5). The two friends worshiped side by side.
Readable says who the crowds were (m2).

source.text: יַשִּׁ֤י מָ֨וֶת׀עָלֵ֗ימוֹ יֵרְד֣וּ שְׁא֣וֹל חַיִּ֑ים כִּֽי־רָע֖וֹת בִּמְגוּרָ֣ם בְּקִרְבָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Let death come by surprise on them; let them go down [to] Sheol alive, for evils [are] in their dwelling, in their midst.

en.L: Let death come on them by surprise; let them go down [to] Sheol alive, for evils [are] in their dwelling, in their midst.
en.B: Let death catch them off guard; let them drop alive into Sheol, for evil lives in their homes and deep within them.
en.R: May death catch these people when they least expect it. May they go down into the place of the dead while they are still alive. Evil is in their homes and in their hearts.

decisions.choice: let death come by surprise: the form to be read
decisions.reason: The written text joins the letters into one word, "desolations"; the form to be read divides them into two words, "let death deceive", that is, come by surprise. The words here follow the form to be read.

decisions.choice: go down alive to Sheol: as Korah did
decisions.reason: When Korah rebelled, the earth opened and he and his followers went down alive to Sheol (Numbers 16). The betrayers are asked to meet the same sudden end (Proverbs 1:12).
Like other psalms, this asks God to judge those who do great wrong. David leaves the judgment to God rather than taking revenge himself (verse 24).
The word (magor) is a place where one lives as a guest or settler.
As in the earlier psalms, Readable explains Sheol.

source.text: אֲ֭נִי אֶל־אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֶקְרָ֑א וַ֝יהוָ֗ה יוֹשִׁיעֵֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: I to God will call, and YHWH will save me.

en.L: As for me, I will call upon God, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will save me.
en.B: But I will cry out to God, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will come to save me.
en.R: But I will pray to God for help, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will rescue me.

decisions.choice: I: in contrast to the betrayers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts "I" first for emphasis: whatever they do, he will turn to God.
This psalm mostly says "God", as the psalms of this part of the book often do, but here it uses both the title and the divine name.
Readable says what calling to God is.

source.text: עֶ֤רֶב וָבֹ֣קֶר וְ֭צָהֳרַיִם אָשִׂ֣יחָה וְאֶהֱמֶ֑ה וַיִּשְׁמַ֥ע קוֹלִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Evening and morning and noon I will complain and moan, and he heard my voice.

en.L: Evening and morning and noon I will complain and moan, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has heard my voice.
en.B: At evening, at morning and at noon I pour out my troubles and groan aloud, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hears me.
en.R: In the evening, in the morning, and at noon, I tell God my troubles and cry. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hears me.

decisions.choice: evening, morning and noon: all day long
decisions.reason: The day began at evening (Genesis 1:5). Praying three times a day was a custom of the devout (Daniel 6).

decisions.choice: and he heard: the answer is sure
decisions.reason: The verb is in the past form: he speaks of God's hearing as already done.
The verb (siach) is that of the noun "complaint" in verse 3.
Readable names whom he tells.

source.text: פָּ֘דָ֤ה בְשָׁל֣וֹם נַ֭פְשִׁי מִקֲּרָב־לִ֑י כִּֽי־בְ֝רַבִּ֗ים הָי֥וּ עִמָּדִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: He has ransomed in peace my soul from [the] battle against me, for in many they were with me.

en.L: He has ransomed my soul in peace from the battle against me, for many were [ranged] with me.
en.B: He has ransomed my life and brought me safely out of the battle waged on me, for many were lined up against me.
en.R: He has saved my life and kept me safe in the fight, even though many people were fighting against me.

decisions.reason: The verb (padah) is to free someone by paying a price; of God, to rescue (25:22; 31:6).
Shalom here is safety: he came out of the fight whole.
"With" here means "fighting with", that is, against (94:16). Some read it as "many were on my side", God's helpers (2 Kings 6:16).
Balanced and Readable give the likely sense (m3).

source.text: יִשְׁמַ֤ע׀אֵ֨ל׀וְֽיַעֲנֵם֮ וְיֹ֤שֵׁ֥ב קֶ֗דֶם סֶ֥לָה אֲשֶׁ֤ר אֵ֣ין חֲלִיפ֣וֹת לָ֑מוֹ וְלֹ֖א יָרְא֣וּ אֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: God will hear and humble them, and [he who] sits [from] of old, Selah, [those] for whom [there are] no changes, and they do not fear God.

en.L: God will hear and humble them, even {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} who sits [enthroned] from of old, those who have no changes and do not fear God. Selah
en.B: God, enthroned since ancient times, will hear and bring them low, for they never change their ways and they do not fear God. Selah
en.R: God has ruled as King since the beginning of time. He will hear what they say and bring them down. They refuse to change, and they have no respect for God. Selah

decisions.reason: The verb can mean "answer" or "humble". After "hear" it may play on both: God hears them and answers by bringing them low.

decisions.choice: sits from of old: enthroned from ancient times
decisions.reason: God sits as King and has always done so (29:10; 93:2).

decisions.choice: no changes: they never change their ways
alternatives: they have no troubles to shake them
decisions.reason: The word (chalifot) means changes. It may mean that they never change their ways, or that life has never shaken them and so they do not fear God.
In the Hebrew, Selah stands in the middle of the verse, after "from of old". Every level puts it at the end so that the sentence is not broken.

decisions.choice: Selah: a word whose meaning is no longer known
alternatives: lift up (the voice or the music)
decisions.reason: Selah stands at the end of a line 71 times in the Psalms and 3 times in Habakkuk 3. It is probably a direction for singing or music, perhaps a pause or an interlude; the ancient Greek translation renders it with a word meaning "interlude". It is not part of what is said, and here it marks a break after the line.
Its meaning is unknown (see the meaning decision on Selah), so every level keeps the word rather than guess, and keeps it apart from the sentence.

source.text: שָׁלַ֣ח יָ֭דָיו בִּשְׁלֹמָ֗יו חִלֵּ֥ל בְּרִיתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: He stretched out his hands against his allies; he profaned his covenant.

en.L: He has stretched out his hands against those at peace with him; he has profaned his covenant.
en.B: My friend has raised his hand against those who were at peace with him; he has broken his covenant.
en.R: My old friend attacked the people who trusted him. He broke the promises he had made.

decisions.reason: The psalm turns back to the betrayer.

decisions.choice: covenant: a sworn bond of friendship
decisions.reason: A covenant could bind friends, as it bound David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18:3). To profane it (chalal) is to treat a sacred bond as nothing.

decisions.choice: allies: those at peace with him
decisions.reason: The word (shelomim) is from shalom: people he had made peace with (7:5).
Balanced and Readable name who is meant (m1).

source.text: חָלְק֤וּ׀מַחְמָאֹ֣ת פִּיו֮ וּֽקֲרָב־לִ֫בּ֥וֹ רַכּ֖וּ דְבָרָ֥יו מִשֶּׁ֗מֶן וְהֵ֣מָּה פְתִחֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: Smooth were [the] butter[y words] of his mouth, but war [was] his heart; softer were his words than oil, yet they [were] drawn swords.

en.L: Smooth were the buttery [words] of his mouth, but war [was in] his heart; his words were softer than oil, but they [were] drawn swords.
en.B: His talk was as smooth as cream, but his heart was set on war; his words flowed more gently than oil, yet each was a drawn sword.
en.R: His words sounded sweet and smooth, but in his heart he wanted to fight. What he said seemed gentle and kind, but his words were really like swords ready to kill.

alternatives: smoother than butter (with the letters divided differently)
decisions.reason: The word (machma'ot) is found only here; it is related to the word for butter or curds. Flattery is smooth speech (5:10; 12:3).
As in 52:4 and 57:5, words are pictured as weapons.
Readable makes the picture a comparison (m2).

source.text: הַשְׁלֵ֤ךְ עַל־יְהוָ֨ה׀יְהָבְךָ֮ וְה֪וּא יְכַ֫לְכְּלֶ֥ךָ לֹא־יִתֵּ֖ן לְעוֹלָ֥ם מ֗וֹט לַצַּדִּֽיק׃

records.literal_gloss: Cast on YHWH your burden, and he will sustain you; not he will allow ever tottering to the righteous.

en.L: Throw on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your burden, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will sustain you; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will not ever allow the righteous to totter.
en.B: Hand over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} whatever weighs on you, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will hold you up; never will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} allow the righteous to stumble and fall.
en.R: Put your troubles in the hands of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will keep you going. He will never let people who do what is right be knocked down.

decisions.choice: burden: what has been given you to carry
decisions.reason: The word (yehav) is found only here; it comes from the verb "give" and may mean the load one has been given. The ancient Greek translation has "your care".
The psalmist turns to the listener, or speaks to himself, and gives the lesson of his own prayer.
"Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you" echoes the ancient Greek translation of this verse.

decisions.choice: totter: be shaken from one's place
decisions.reason: The verb (mot) is that of verse 4: the enemies make trouble totter onto him, but God will not let the righteous totter.

decisions.choice: people who do what is right
decisions.reason: As in the earlier psalms, Readable explains tsaddiq.

source.text: וְאַתָּ֤ה אֱלֹהִ֨ים׀תּוֹרִדֵ֬ם׀לִבְאֵ֬ר שַׁ֗חַת אַנְשֵׁ֤י דָמִ֣ים וּ֭מִרְמָה לֹא־יֶחֱצ֣וּ יְמֵיהֶ֑ם וַ֝אֲנִ֗י אֶבְטַח־בָּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And you, God, will bring them down to [the] well of [the] pit; men of bloods and deceit will not halve their days; and I will trust in you.

en.L: But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, God, will bring them down to the well of the pit; {{gender:people|men}} of bloodshed and deceit will not live half their days; but I will trust in {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.
en.B: But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, God, will send them down to the deepest pit; killers and liars will not see even half their years. As for me, I will trust in {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.
en.R: But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, God, will throw them down into the grave. People who murder and lie will die young. But I will trust in {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.

decisions.choice: the well of the pit: the grave
decisions.reason: The pit is the grave and the world of the dead (28:1; 30:4). It is pictured as a deep well one cannot climb out of.

decisions.choice: not halve their days: die before their time
decisions.reason: They will not reach the middle of a normal life (102:25).

decisions.choice: men of bloods: people who shed blood
decisions.reason: As in 5:7 and 26:9: murderers. "Bloods" is plural as in 51:16.

decisions.choice: but I: the psalm's last word
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts "I" first again, as in verse 17. The psalm ends with trust.
The phrase means anyone who sheds blood, men and women alike.
Readable says what the idiom means (m2).
